div.head: Leis Wl 10, 10a
div.ab: Si hom fait plaie en auter e il deive faire les amendes, primereinement lui rende sien lecheof. [10a] E li plaez jurra sur seinz, que pur meins nel pot feire ne pur haur si cher nel fist.
Si home fait plaie a altre e il de[iv]e otrei faire les amendes, primerement li rende sun lechefe. [10a] E li plaiez jurra[d] sur seintz, que pur me[n]s nel pot faire ne pur haur si chier nel fist.

De uulnerante alium. Si uulnerauerit quis alium et satisfacere debeat, imprimis reddat ei lichfe, quantum scilicet in curam uulneris impendit. [10a] Iurabit tamen uulneratus, quod non potuit pro minori illud curasse, nec quod in odium illius magis iusto persoluit.
Si hom fait plaie [a] auter e il deive faire les amendes, primereinement lui rende sien leche[feo]. E li plaez jurra sur seinz que pur meins nel pot feire ne pur haur si cher nel fist.

10. Wenn jemand einem anderen eine Wunde zufügt und er soll (dem anderen I) die Busse zahlen, so gebe er ihm zuerst dessen Arztkosten. [10a] 10a. Und der Verwundete soll auf die Heiligen [Reliquien] schwören, dass er es für Geringeres nicht thun konnte, noch es aus Hass so theuer gemacht hat.

10. If someone inflicts a wound on another and he is to pay the compensation (to the other I), then he shall first give him his physician's costs. [10a] 10a. And the wounded man shall swear on the saints [relics] that he could not have done it for less, nor has made it so dear out of hatred.

If a man wounds another and has to pay compensation, he shall, in the first instance, pay the cost of his medical attendance. And the wounded man shall swear on the holy relics that he could not do it for less, and that he has not increased the amount out of malice.
div.note: Added October 2026 from Robertson pp. 258–259 (text and translation); Robertson's 10; Liebermann divides it into 10 and 10a (at E li plaez jurra).; Liebermann’s text and German translation added from Gesetze I p. 498–501, October 2026 (two independent readings of the page images)

note.seg: die Quelle von 10—10, 2 (wohl Angelsächsisch, laut læcefeoh und sarbot) beeinflusste Libertates de Prestona in Aumundrenesse, ein seit Edward I. überliefertes, inhaltlich älteres, Stadtrecht (ed. Bateson Engl. hist. rev. 1900, 498. 501): . . . 21. Item si burgensis vulnerat alium, et voluerint concordare, amici inter eos positi seruent [bessere decernent oder Synonymes] pro unoquoque police plage cooperte IIII denarios, pro discooperto octo denarios; et quicquid vulneratus per disturbacionem plage sue poterit probare quod perdidit, alius ei reddet; et similiter quod vulneratus dedit medico suo pro sanacione plage, ei reddet; et arma ei afferet et iurabit super arma: ‘si vulneratus esset, et [jener] ei talia fecisset, ipse caperet quod ei offert, si amici sui hoc consenserint et laudarent’.

the source of 10—10, 2 (probably Anglo-Saxon, judging by læcefeoh and sarbot) influenced the Libertates de Prestona in Aumundrenesse, a town law transmitted from Edward I's time onwards but older in its content (ed. Bateson Engl. hist. rev. 1900, 498. 501): . . . 21. Item si burgensis vulnerat alium, et voluerint concordare, amici inter eos positi seruent [read decernent or a synonym] pro unoquoque police plage cooperte IIII denarios, pro discooperto octo denarios; et quicquid vulneratus per disturbacionem plage sue poterit probare quod perdidit, alius ei reddet; et similiter quod vulneratus dedit medico suo pro sanacione plage, ei reddet; et arma ei afferet et iurabit super arma: ‘si vulneratus esset, et [the other] ei talia fecisset, ipse caperet quod ei offert, si amici sui hoc consenserint et laudarent’.

Vor der Gliederbusse.—Das Wort læcefeoh (s. Wb) hat nichts mit lic oder gefe zu tun [gegen Schmid 624; Stephens Blandinger I 217]; vgl. Ps.-Egb. Confess. 22 (aus Fränk. Bussbuch ed. Wasserschleben 309): forgylde die Wunde ⁊ þæt læcefeoh þam læce gylde; ed. Thorpe Anc. laws 352; ähnlich gif hwylc oðerne wundige, gebete wið hine þa wúnde ⁊ begyte him þa lácnunge; Poen. Ps.-Egb. IV 22 und Beda: Qui deformem hominem reddidit, inpensas in medicum et macule precium; Poenit. IV 9 ed. Wasserschleben 225; daraus Ps.-Beda ebd. 265, Fränk. Ps.-Theodor ebd. 588.—Das Wort mag zwar Nordischem læknisfeh entlehnt sein (Toller; Steenstrup [Danelag 314] vergleicht Jütisch lækigiaf; s. auch Seebohm Tribal Agsax. 241). Die Sache aber kennen auch Franken, Langobarden u. a.; Brunner II 613f; Pol Mai II 524; Schreuer Verbrechenskonk. 26; Gl Arzt 2ff.

Before the compensation for limbs.—The word læcefeoh (see Wb) has nothing to do with lic or gefe [against Schmid 624; Stephens Blandinger I 217]; cf. Ps.-Egb. Confess. 22 (from a Frankish penitential (Bussbuch) ed. Wasserschleben 309): forgylde the wound ⁊ þæt læcefeoh þam læce gylde; ed. Thorpe Anc. laws 352; similarly gif hwylc oðerne wundige, gebete wið hine þa wúnde ⁊ begyte him þa lácnunge; Poen. Ps.-Egb. IV 22, and Beda: Qui deformem hominem reddidit, inpensas in medicum et macule precium; Poenit. IV 9 ed. Wasserschleben 225; whence Ps.-Beda ibid. 265, the Frankish Ps.-Theodor ibid. 588.—The word may indeed be borrowed from Norse læknisfeh (Toller; Steenstrup [Danelag 314] compares Jutish lækigiaf; see also Seebohm Tribal Agsax. 241). The thing itself, however, is known also to the Franks, the Lombards and others; Brunner II 613f; Pol Mai II 524; Schreuer Verbrechenskonk. 26; Gl Arzt 2ff.
